summary: Describes how IPv4 and IPv6 SIP user agents communicate at the signaling layer and exchange media, including single- and dual-stack agents. It updates RFC 3264 and is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone using old-style addresses and one using new-style addresses need a way to call each other. This explains how.

questions: how does sip work between ipv4 and ipv6
what is a dual-stack sip proxy
why use ice for ipv6 sip
subtitle: How SIP calls get signaling and media across the gap between IPv4-only and IPv6-only phones.

tldr.problem: SIP signaling can cross between IPv4 and IPv6 networks, but the media (such as audio) that follows cannot, because an IPv4-only user agent cannot send to an IPv6 address and often cannot even parse one.
tldr.mechanism: Domains run dual-stack proxies that stay in the signaling path with Record-Route, and user agents gather both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses with ICE (using relays where needed) so every offer is usable by either side.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 and IPv6 user agents can set up sessions with each other while the installed IPv4 base stays unchanged. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3264.

today: RFC 6157 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2011. It updates RFC 3264, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Two Layers to Transition
sections.content:
SIP sets up and manages multimedia sessions. After the signaling messages are exchanged, the endpoints send the actual session traffic, which is not carried by SIP. Audio streams, for example, are typically carried with the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP).

A complete IPv6 transition therefore has to work at two layers. The RFC says that unextended SIP can already handle mixed IPv6/IPv4 networks at the signaling layer, as long as proxy servers and their DNS entries are properly configured. At the media layer, user agents on different networks must implement extensions before they can exchange media.

The document defines terms for the cast: IPv4-only, IPv6-only and IPv4/IPv6 (dual-stack) nodes and user agents, plus the IPv4/IPv6 proxy that supports SIP signaling on both networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Making a call has two parts: first you ring the bell, then you talk. The bell part mostly works already, but the talking part needs some extra help when the two sides use different kinds of addresses.

sections.title: Dual-Stack Proxies and DNS
sections.content:
User agents usually send SIP traffic to an outbound proxy. The RFC RECOMMENDED that domains deploy dual-stack outbound proxies, or else both IPv4-only and IPv6-only outbound proxies. There SHOULD be both IPv4 and IPv6 DNS entries for outbound proxies, so each user agent can find the address that suits it: an IPv4-only agent asks for A records, an IPv6-only agent asks for AAAA records, and a dual-stack agent asks for all records and picks a network.

Domains are also RECOMMENDED to provide discovery mechanisms that hand out both IPv4 and IPv6 proxy addresses, for example the DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options for SIP servers.

The same advice applies to the inbound proxy that receives traffic from outside the domain. A dual-stack proxy also lets an IPv6-only agent in the domain signal an IPv4-only agent in the same domain. Without such a proxy, user agents on different networks cannot successfully signal each other.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office needs a front desk that can read both address styles, and the phone book should list both versions of its address, so everyone can find the one they can use.

sections.title: Relaying Between Networks with Record-Route
sections.content:
A proxy that receives a request over IPv6 and relays it over IPv4 (or the reverse) must stay in the path of later requests, because otherwise the upstream client and the downstream server cannot talk directly. So such a proxy MUST be configured to Record-Route.

How many Record-Route headers it inserts depends on what it puts in them. If the URI holds a fully qualified domain name that has both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in DNS, one header is enough. If it holds an IP address, the proxy must insert two: the first with the address compatible with the downstream server's network, the second with the address compatible with the upstream client.

In the RFC's example, proxy P (192.0.2.1 on IPv4, 2001:db8::1 on IPv6) relays an INVITE from an IPv4 client to an IPv6 server. The server's route set starts with the proxy's IPv6 address, and the client, which reverses the Record-Route headers as RFC 3261 requires, ends up with the proxy's IPv4 address first. Both can then reach the proxy.

The RFC warns that an RFC 2543 endpoint may fail here, since that specification's ABNF had no rules for parsing IPv6 identifiers. This is generally not a problem for RFC 3261 endpoints, even on an IPv4-only node.
sections.plainLanguage: When the post office passes a letter between the two styles, it keeps its name on the envelope so replies come back through it. It writes its address in both styles so each side sees the one it can read.

sections.title: The Media Problem and ICE
sections.content:
SIP sets up media with the offer/answer model: the offerer sends a session description (usually in SDP) with codecs and transport addresses, and the answerer replies with what it will use. A direct exchange between an IPv4-only and an IPv6-only agent fails, because the IPv4-only agent cannot send media to IPv6 addresses and generally does not understand their format.

The RFC puts the greater burden on IPv6 agents, which are expected to be dual-stacked anyway, so the installed IPv4 base keeps working unchanged. An IPv6 node SHOULD be able to send and receive media over IPv4, and if it cannot, it SHOULD support the STUN relay usage so a relay can send and receive IPv4 media for it. The cost is that an operator introducing IPv6 must provide extra relay servers, though operators often have STUN relays for NAT traversal already.

Some nodes run as IPv6-only even though they support both, for example where public IPv4 addresses are scarce or where the link layer does not support IPv4 and IPv6 at once.

Addresses are gathered with the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) procedures. IPv4/IPv6 agents SHOULD gather both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses for all their offers, so any answerer can build an acceptable answer, which also shortens setup. Once the answer is made, both sides run ICE connectivity checks, which help prevent some flooding attacks. ICE can be skipped inside a managed network where the administrator controls the IP version of every node.
sections.plainLanguage: If one friend can only read old-style addresses, the new-style friend has to give a helper-address in the old style. Offering both kinds up front means whoever answers can pick the one they can use.

sections.title: Updates to RFC 3264
sections.content:
The RFC makes two normative changes to the offer/answer rules of RFC 3264.

  • When an offer needs the IPv6 equivalent of the IPv4 unspecified address 0.0.0.0 (seen with third party call control), IPv6 implementations MUST use a domain name in the .invalid top-level domain instead of the IPv6 unspecified address ::.
  • Each media description in an answer MUST use the same network type as the matching media description in the offer. If the offer's c= line says IP4, the answer's says IP4; if it says IP6, the answer says IP6.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two new rules: use a special made-up name when you mean 'no address yet', and answer in the same address style the question used.

sections.title: Choosing Which Server Address to Try
sections.content:
RFC 3263 maps a SIP URI to a set of DNS SRV records, ordered by priority and then by weight. The client then does an A or AAAA lookup on the target it found. IPv6-only or dual-stack clients MUST use getaddrinfo() rather than gethostbyname() for this, because the newer function implements the source and destination address selection algorithms of RFC 3484. Proxies and user agents must follow these recommendations when ordering the servers they contact.

The benefit is an ordered list of IPv6 and IPv4 destinations based on how good each source and destination pair is. The cost is dependence on broad operating system support and uniform implementation of the APIs. The RFC points developers to known problems: getaddrinfo() may put IPv6 global addresses first even when the host only has an IPv6 link-local scope and an IPv4 address, which delays connection.
sections.plainLanguage: When the phone book gives several addresses, your phone uses a smart helper to put them in the best order to try, instead of just taking the first one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures here use other protocols (STUN relay usage, ICE, SDP), and each one's threat model is in its own document. The RFC says the new procedures introduce no new security threats, but they may make hosts more amenable to existing ones.

Its example is a user agent client that allocates both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address and puts them in the SDP. A malicious agent that intercepts the request could mount a denial-of-service attack aimed at the different network interfaces. The client should then protect confidentiality and integrity of messages, using the SIPS URI scheme or secure MIME from RFC 3261. If HTTP Digest authentication is used, the quality of protection should also cover the SDP payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling people more than one way to reach you also gives a prankster more doors to knock on, so you should send the details in a sealed envelope.
